set1.q: A 30-year-old man has used an over-the-counter redness-relief drop every day for a month. His eyes are redder than when he started. What has happened?
opts: Rebound hyperemia
Correct. Beyond about two weeks, stopping leaves the eye redder than it started. This is the counseling point most worth carrying out of this topic.
He has bacterial conjunctivitis
Nothing here suggests infection, and the timing follows the drop rather than an exposure.
The drops have raised his intraocular pressure
Raised pressure is a steroid and non-steroidal concern, not a vasoconstrictor one.
He has developed allergic conjunctivitis
Possible in general, but the history of daily vasoconstrictor use for a month points squarely at rebound.

set1.q: A 49-year-old woman starting a prostaglandin analog in one eye should be warned about which cosmetic effects?
opts: Longer lashes and iris color change
Correct, and they matter more when only one eye is treated. Conjunctival hyperemia is common too.
Drooping of the eyelid
Eyelid drooping is not among the effects listed for the prostaglandin analogs; the effects to warn about are longer lashes, iris color change and conjunctival hyperemia.
Yellowing of the sclera
Yellowing of the sclera is not an effect of the prostaglandin analogs.
Permanent pupil dilation
Permanent dilation is not an effect of this class; the changes are to lashes and iris color.

set1.q: An 18-month-old needs pressure-lowering therapy. Which class is contraindicated?
opts: Prostaglandin analogs
Prostaglandin analogs carry no stated age contraindication; the under-two rule is the alpha-2 agonists.
Carbonic anhydrase inhibitors
Carbonic anhydrase inhibitors cause bitter taste and stinging rather than apnea and have no stated age ban; the class contraindicated under two years is the alpha-2 agonists.
Alpha-2 agonists
Correct — contraindicated under two years because of central nervous system depression and apnea.
Cholinergic agonists
Cholinergic agonists cause miosis and blurred vision rather than apnea and have no stated age ban; the class contraindicated under two years is the alpha-2 agonists.

set1.q: A 71-year-old on dorzolamide complains of a persistent bitter taste and stinging on instillation. What do you tell him?
opts: This suggests an allergy and the drug must stop
Allergic conjunctivitis can occur, but taste and stinging are expected effects.
This means the drop is contaminated
A bitter taste and stinging are known, expected effects of dorzolamide rather than signs of contamination; warning patients in advance improves adherence.
This indicates systemic absorption and cardiac risk
Cardiac risk belongs to the beta blocker drops; taste and stinging are the expected local effects of a carbonic anhydrase inhibitor and do not signal cardiac harm.
Both are common with this class
Correct, and they are common enough that warning in advance improves adherence. Bitter taste in about a quarter and stinging in about a third.

set1.q: A patient is being taught to instill an eye drop. What is named as the single most important step?
opts: Tilting the head back to form a lower lid pocket
Necessary, but it is step three; the hand washing is what is singled out.
Holding the eyes closed for two to three minutes
Important for keeping drug in contact with the eye, but not the step highlighted as most important.
Washing the hands thoroughly with soap and water
Correct. It is marked as the most important step, and it comes before anything else. The dropper must then not touch anything, so it stays sterile.
Covering the lacrimal duct after instilling
It reduces systemic absorption and drainage, and is genuinely useful — but again not the step marked most important.

set1.q: A 47-year-old farm worker develops fungal keratitis after a corneal injury with plant material. Which commercially available ophthalmic agent treats it?
opts: Trifluridine
Trifluridine is an antiviral for herpes simplex keratitis and has no antifungal action; natamycin is the commercially available ophthalmic antifungal.
Amphotericin B drops
Used ophthalmically but not as a commercially available product; it must be compounded.
Oral fluconazole alone
Systemic azoles have a role, but the question asks for the available ophthalmic agent.
Natamycin
Correct — the only commercially available ophthalmic antifungal. It covers Aspergillus, Candida, Cephalosporium, Fusarium and Penicillium.

set1.q: A 55-year-old has been using tobramycin drops for five days and now has worsening pain and a corneal defect. What has happened?
opts: Rebound hyperemia
Rebound hyperemia follows stopping an alpha-agonist redness-relief drop; an antibiotic that leaves a corneal defect points to corneal ulceration from an aminoglycoside.
Corneal ulceration
Correct, along with reactive keratoconjunctivitis. It is one of the few ocular adverse effects specific enough to name a class.
Ordinary ocular irritation, common to all ophthalmic antibiotics
Irritation is indeed common to all of them, which is why it is NOT the answer when a specific defect has appeared.
A white precipitate from the drug
That belongs to ciprofloxacin and is a surface deposit, not an ulcer.

set1.q: A newborn needs prophylaxis against ophthalmia neonatorum. Which agent?
opts: Erythromycin ointment
Correct. It is the named agent for newborn prophylaxis, and it is inexpensive.
Azithromycin solution
Azithromycin solution is used for conjunctivitis and is considerably more expensive; the inexpensive named agent for newborn prophylaxis is erythromycin ointment.
Moxifloxacin solution
Moxifloxacin is a fluoroquinolone kept for conjunctivitis and corneal ulcers, not newborn prophylaxis; erythromycin ointment is the named agent.
Natamycin suspension
Natamycin is an antifungal and has no role in preventing neonatal bacterial conjunctivitis; erythromycin ointment is the named agent.

set1.q: Why are younger patients usually intolerant of miotic therapy?
opts: Systemic bradycardia from muscarinic activation
Systemic bradycardia is not the reason given. What young patients cannot tolerate is the visual blurring from induced myopia.
Visual blurring from induced myopia
Correct. Fixed small pupils, induced myopia and visual disturbance are the effects, and a young eye with active accommodation notices them most. That, plus frequent dosing, is why compliance is poor.
Permanent iris color change
Permanent iris color change is a prostaglandin analog effect and has nothing to do with muscarinic agonists.
Increased airway resistance
Increased airway resistance is a non-selective beta blocker concern, mediated by beta-2 blockade in the lung.

set1.q: What is the central instruction for a patient given a topical nasal decongestant?
set1.io: Topic — Lecture 5: Ear, Nose and Throat Drugs
opts: Do not use it beyond a few days
Correct. It is the whole safety message for this drug, and exceeding it is what produces rebound congestion.
Use it every day through the allergy season
Continuous use is exactly what causes the problem; beyond a few days the spray produces rebound congestion.
Use it only at night
Timing is not the restriction. The restriction is on duration: no more than a few days of use.
Always combine it with a nasal steroid
Combining nasal sprays is specifically discouraged, and it does nothing about the duration limit that matters here.

set1.q: A patient with diabetes is started on a course of prednisone. What should be anticipated?
set1.io: Topic — Lecture 5: Ear, Nose and Throat Drugs
opts: Glucose will fall and treatment may need reducing
Corticosteroids raise glucose rather than lowering it, and they also reduce the effect of antidiabetic medicines.
There is no interaction with antidiabetic medicines
A reduced effect on antidiabetic treatment is specifically described.
Glucose control will worsen
Correct. Two effects pointing the same way: the steroid raises glucose and blunts the drugs used to lower it. Antidiabetic medicines will work less well.
Insulin requirements will fall
They would be expected to rise: the steroid raises glucose and blunts the drugs used to lower it.

set1.q: Why must a benzonatate capsule be swallowed whole?
set1.io: Topic — Lecture 5: Ear, Nose and Throat Drugs
opts: Chewing destroys the active drug before it works
The problem is where the drug acts rather than loss of activity: chewing releases local anesthetic into the mouth and throat.
Chewing causes irritation of the stomach lining
Gastric irritation is not the stated reason. Chewing releases anesthetic where it will numb the airway.
It releases local anesthetic into the mouth
Correct. Benzonatate is a local anesthetic, so chewing the capsule releases it in the mouth and throat, numbing the airway a patient needs to protect, and the drug then does not treat the cough.
Chewing gives the medicine a bitter taste
The concern is anesthesia rather than taste: released in the mouth, it numbs whatever it touches.

set1.q: A child with acute otitis media has a penicillin allergy. Which agents are offered?
set1.io: Topic — Lecture 5: Ear, Nose and Throat Drugs
opts: Cefdinir or azithromycin
Correct. Both are listed, though the macrolide is the weaker of the two here because pneumococcal resistance to macrolides runs high.
Ciprofloxacin or levofloxacin
Fluoroquinolones are not the listed oral option for this infection in children.
Clindamycin or cefixime
That pairing belongs to bacterial rhinosinusitis in a penicillin-allergic patient.
Vancomycin or linezolid
These are not among the agents used for uncomplicated acute otitis media.

set1.q: A patient on a diuretic is started on dexamethasone. What should be monitored?
set1.io: Topic — Lecture 5: Ear, Nose and Throat Drugs
opts: Liver enzymes and bilirubin
Not the concern in this combination. Both a diuretic and dexamethasone lower potassium, so potassium is what to monitor.
Thyroid function tests
Not the concern in this combination; potassium is, since both drugs push it the same way.
Potassium, since both drugs lower it
Correct. Two drugs pushing the same electrolyte the same way, which is how a patient arrives at a dangerous level without either drug being at fault alone.
Prothrombin time and clotting
Not relevant to this pairing. Potassium is the shared target of a diuretic and a corticosteroid.

set1.q: Why is a patient who has taken a corticosteroid for more than about a week told not to stop abruptly?
set1.io: Topic — Lecture 5: Ear, Nose and Throat Drugs
opts: The drug accumulates and must be cleared slowly
Accumulation is not the reason given. Stopping abruptly after more than about a week produces rebound symptoms.
Abrupt withdrawal causes fluid retention
Fluid retention is an effect of taking the drug, not of stopping it.
The drug loses effect if restarted after a gap
Loss of future effect is not the concern. Abrupt withdrawal after a week or more produces rebound symptoms.
Stopping suddenly produces rebound symptoms
Correct. After more than about a week of use, stopping suddenly produces rebound symptoms, so the drug is tapered instead; a short course and a long course are stopped differently.

set1.q: Which patient must not be given dextromethorphan?
set1.io: Topic — Lecture 5: Ear, Nose and Throat Drugs
opts: One taking an oral antihistamine
Not a contraindication. The contraindication is a monoamine oxidase inhibitor, currently or within the past two weeks.
One taking a monoamine oxidase inhibitor
Correct. The restriction runs for two weeks after stopping a monoamine oxidase inhibitor, which is the part most easily missed because the patient has already stopped the drug.
One with treated hypertension
Not the stated contraindication, which is current or recent use of a monoamine oxidase inhibitor.
One with a productive, chesty cough
That is a reason to question the choice rather than a contraindication.

set1.q: What is the standard of therapy for acute bacterial rhinosinusitis?
set1.io: Topic — Lecture 5: Ear, Nose and Throat Drugs
opts: High-dose amoxicillin alone
That is the otitis media starting point; sinusitis begins a step further along.
Azithromycin
Not the standard of therapy for this infection. Amoxicillin-clavulanate is, because beta-lactamase producing Haemophilus influenzae is common here.
Doxycycline
Not among the agents offered here. The standard is amoxicillin-clavulanate, with clindamycin plus cefixime or levofloxacin for penicillin allergy.
Amoxicillin-clavulanate
Correct. Unlike otitis media, this one starts with the clavulanate already on board, because beta-lactamase producing Haemophilus influenzae is common here.

set1.q: Which patients should avoid ibuprofen?
set1.io: Topic — Lecture 5: Ear, Nose and Throat Drugs
opts: Those with a history of Reye's syndrome
Reye's relates to aspirin in children rather than to ibuprofen.
Those with asthma it may worsen

Correct. Asthma is the one most easily forgotten because it is not an obvious consequence of blocking prostaglandin synthesis; previous ulcer or perforation and renal impairment are the other contraindications.
Those taking acetaminophen
Acetaminophen is not a contraindication to ibuprofen. The contraindications are asthma, prior ulcer or perforation, and renal impairment.
Those over sixty-five years old
Age alone is not the stated contraindication; asthma, previous ulceration and renal impairment are, along with very young infants.

set1.q: Which beta blocker is indicated for heart failure?
opts: Propranolol
Propranolol is a non-selective agent used for migraine prophylaxis; it is not one of the heart failure three (carvedilol, metoprolol succinate, bisoprolol).
Bisoprolol
Correct. The three beta blockers used for heart failure are carvedilol, metoprolol succinate and bisoprolol.
Atenolol
Atenolol is beta-1 selective but not one of the heart failure agents. Those are carvedilol, metoprolol succinate and bisoprolol.
Nadolol
Nadolol is a non-selective, first-generation agent. The heart failure beta blockers are carvedilol, metoprolol succinate and bisoprolol.

set1.q: In a patient with renal disease whose renal blood flow depends on angiotensin II, what can happen when an ACE (angiotensin-converting enzyme) inhibitor is started?
opts: Filtration rate rises sharply
The change is a fall, not a rise: removing angiotensin II takes away the support that kept glomerular pressure up in these kidneys.
Renal blood flow is unchanged
Renal blood flow is not spared in these patients; the loss of angiotensin II can dramatically decrease glomerular filtration.
Potassium falls sharply
Potassium tends to rise on this class, especially with renal disease. The kidney-specific danger is a dramatic fall in filtration.
Filtration rate drops sharply
Correct. Where renal blood flow depends on angiotensin II, ACE inhibitors can dramatically decrease the glomerular filtration rate, so they are used cautiously and titrated slowly.

set1.q: A patient in her third trimester cannot take an ACE (angiotensin-converting enzyme) inhibitor. Is an angiotensin receptor blocker an acceptable substitute?
opts: Yes, it spares the fetus
It does not spare the fetus. Angiotensin receptor blockers carry the same fetal morbidity and mortality and are not given in trimesters two and three.
Yes, at a reduced dose
Dose reduction does not make it safe. The class is not given in the second and third trimesters because of fetal harm.
No, it is also avoided then
Correct. Angiotensin receptor blockers share the fetal morbidity and mortality and are not given in the second and third trimesters.
Only if potassium is normal
Potassium is not the deciding factor. The class is avoided in the second and third trimesters because of fetal morbidity and mortality.

set1.q: During a nitroprusside infusion, a patient develops trembling, vomiting and convulsions. Sodium thiosulfate is given. Which toxicity does it limit?
opts: Thiocyanate toxicity
Thiocyanate toxicity causes weakness, anoxia, tinnitus, muscle spasms and toxic psychosis with long infusions or renal failure; thiosulfate is given for cyanide.
Cyanide toxicity
Correct. Each nitroprusside molecule carries five cyanide groups; cyanide toxicity causes trembling, vomiting and convulsions, and sodium thiosulfate limits it.
Lupus syndrome
Lupus syndrome is a hydralazine toxicity of long-term, high-dose use. The infusion toxicity that thiosulfate limits is cyanide.
Hyperkalemia
Hyperkalemia is not a nitroprusside toxicity. Sodium thiosulfate is given to limit cyanide toxicity.

set1.q: A patient recently started on prazosin feels lightheaded every time he stands up. What is the most likely cause?
opts: Orthostatic hypotension
Correct. Orthostatic hypotension with postural dizziness is the leading prazosin side effect, alongside headache, drowsiness and lack of energy.
Reflex bradycardia
Prazosin produces a mild reflex tachycardia, not bradycardia. Dizziness on standing is orthostatic hypotension.
First-dose hyperkalemia
Hyperkalemia belongs to ACE (angiotensin-converting enzyme) inhibitors and angiotensin receptor blockers, not prazosin, whose standing dizziness is orthostatic.
Central sedation
Drowsiness can occur, but dizziness specifically on standing is orthostatic hypotension from alpha-1 blockade.

set1.q: Which condition is a contraindication to diltiazem?
opts: Supraventricular tachycardia
Supraventricular tachycardia is an approved indication for diltiazem, not a contraindication; nodal slowing is what treats it.
Chronic stable angina
Angina is an approved indication for diltiazem. The contraindication is advanced heart block, which its nodal suppression would worsen.
Uncomplicated hypertension
Hypertension is an approved indication. Diltiazem is contraindicated in advanced heart block and hypotension.
Advanced heart block
Correct. Advanced heart block and hypotension are contraindications; heart failure, liver disease and gastroesophageal reflux disease are relative contraindications.

set1.q: A patient takes nadolol. How is it classified?
opts: Beta-1 selective blocker
The beta-1 selective (second-generation) agents are acebutolol, atenolol, bisoprolol, esmolol and metoprolol. Nadolol is non-selective.
Non-selective beta blocker
Correct. Nadolol is one of the first-generation, non-selective agents, with propranolol, penbutolol, pindolol, sotalol and timolol.
Alpha-1 and beta blocker
The agents that add alpha-1 blockade are the third-generation carvedilol and labetalol. Nadolol is a first-generation, non-selective beta blocker.
Central alpha-2 agonist
Central alpha-2 agonists are clonidine and guanfacine. Nadolol ends in -lol and is a non-selective beta blocker.

set1.q: A patient with type 1 diabetes is starting propranolol. What should he be told about hypoglycemia?
opts: Warning signs may be masked
Correct. Beta blockers inhibit glycogenolysis, so hypoglycemia lasts longer, and they mask its adrenergic warning symptoms.
It will become less frequent
Beta blockers do not protect against hypoglycemia; by inhibiting glycogenolysis they prolong it and hide its warning signs.
Insulin will no longer be needed
Beta blockers do not replace insulin. The warning is that hypoglycemia may be prolonged and its symptoms masked.
Blood sugar will run high only
In type 2 diabetes reduced insulin can raise glucose, but the danger stressed for any diabetic is prolonged, masked hypoglycemia.

set1.q: A 68-year-old man has benign prostatic hyperplasia and hypertension. Which single drug treats both?
opts: Tamsulosin
Tamsulosin treats benign prostatic hyperplasia but has limited vascular effects because it is alpha-1A selective, so it is not the antihypertensive choice.
Clonidine
Clonidine lowers blood pressure centrally but has no prostate indication. Terazosin treats both conditions.
Terazosin
Correct. The other alpha-1 selective agents, terazosin and doxazosin, are used both as antihypertensives and for benign prostatic hyperplasia.
Amlodipine
Amlodipine treats hypertension and angina but not prostatic hyperplasia. An alpha-1 blocker such as terazosin treats both.

set1.q: Which form of niacin is NOT effective as an antilipemic?
opts: Niacinamide
Correct. Niacin is a B-complex vitamin; nicotinic acid is the antilipemic form, and its amide, niacinamide (nicotinamide), is not effective.
Nicotinic acid
Nicotinic acid is the form used as an antilipemic. The amide form, niacinamide, is the ineffective one.
Extended-release niacin
Extended-release niacin is a prescription antilipemic product. Niacinamide is the form that does not work.
Immediate-release niacin
Immediate-release niacin is an antilipemic product (a supplement or by prescription). Niacinamide is ineffective.

set1.q: How does the ACC/AHA (American College of Cardiology/American Heart Association) cholesterol guideline differ from ATP III (Adult Treatment Panel III)?
opts: It targets an LDL below 100 mg/dL
An LDL under 100 mg/dL as the optimal goal is the ATP III approach, which the newer guideline dropped.
It starts everyone on high intensity
The newer guideline starts either moderate- or high-intensity statin therapy for the four groups, not high intensity for all.
It makes niacin the first choice
Statins remain first line; the change was dropping titration to an LDL target.
It does not treat to an LDL target
Correct. It starts moderate- or high-intensity statin therapy for the four benefit groups and does not titrate to a specific LDL (low-density lipoprotein) target.

set1.q: Which of these statins is one of the two that can reach high intensity?
opts: Simvastatin
Simvastatin reaches moderate or low intensity only. Atorvastatin and rosuvastatin are the high-intensity statins.
Pitavastatin
Pitavastatin is listed only as moderate intensity. The two high-intensity statins are atorvastatin and rosuvastatin.
Atorvastatin
Correct. Atorvastatin and rosuvastatin are the only statins that reach high intensity (50% or greater lowering of LDL, low-density lipoprotein, cholesterol).
Pravastatin
Pravastatin is moderate or low intensity. Only atorvastatin and rosuvastatin reach high intensity.

set1.q: Which description fits alirocumab?
opts: Oral bile acid-binding resin
Oral resins are cholestyramine, colestipol and colesevelam. Alirocumab is an injectable monoclonal antibody.
Injectable monoclonal antibody
Correct. Alirocumab and evolocumab are injectable-only monoclonal antibodies, and they are expensive.
Oral HMG-CoA reductase inhibitor
Oral HMG-CoA reductase inhibitors are the statins. Alirocumab is an injectable monoclonal antibody against PCSK9.
Oral cholesterol absorption blocker
The oral cholesterol absorption inhibitor is ezetimibe. Alirocumab is an injectable monoclonal antibody.

set1.q: A patient on simvastatin develops muscle toxicity. What is required?
opts: Continue and add a fibrate
Fibrates add to statin myopathy risk. Muscle toxicity requires the statin to be discontinued.
Double the dose briefly
A higher dose raises myopathy risk. Muscle toxicity requires discontinuing the statin.
Switch to taking it with grapefruit
Grapefruit juice raises statin levels through CYP3A4 and would worsen toxicity. The statin must be stopped.
Discontinue the statin
Correct. The presence of muscle toxicity requires discontinuing the statin; myopathy occurs in 0.2 to 0.4% with rare rhabdomyolysis.

set1.q: A patient on warfarin is started on gemfibrozil. Which interaction is expected?
opts: Reduced warfarin absorption
Reduced warfarin absorption is the bile acid sequestrant interaction, avoided by separating the doses. Fibrates increase warfarin's effect.
Increased anticoagulant effect
Correct. Fibrates increase the anticoagulant effect of warfarin; they also interact with statins, ezetimibe and bile acid sequestrants.
Reduced anticoagulant effect
The direction is the reverse: fibrates increase the anticoagulant effect of warfarin.
No interaction is expected
There is a listed interaction: fibrates increase warfarin's anticoagulant effect.

set1.q: Which is an ABSOLUTE contraindication to niacin?
opts: Chronic liver disease
Correct. Chronic liver disease is the absolute contraindication; peptic ulcer disease, symptomatic gout, significant hyperuricemia and diabetes are relative ones.
Peptic ulcer disease
Peptic ulcer disease is a relative, not absolute, contraindication to niacin. Chronic liver disease is absolute.
History of symptomatic gout
Symptomatic gout is a relative contraindication, because niacin raises uric acid. Chronic liver disease is absolute.
Diabetes with glucose intolerance
Diabetes is a relative contraindication, since niacin decreases glucose tolerance. Chronic liver disease is absolute.

set1.q: Why are bile acid sequestrants approved for children, adolescents and pregnancy?
opts: They are cleared quickly by the kidney
Renal clearance is not the reason. Resins are not absorbed at all, so they cause few systemic effects.
They are not absorbed from the gut
Correct. Because resins stay in the gastrointestinal tract, systemic side effects are limited; they are called the safest drug for that reason.
They have no effect on other drugs
Resins do affect other drugs, binding digoxin, warfarin, thyroxine, beta blockers and thiazides. Their safety comes from not being absorbed.
They have no gastrointestinal effects
Gastrointestinal effects are common: bloating, flatulence, fullness, constipation and nausea. Their safety comes from not being absorbed.

set1.q: In which patient is a fibrate contraindicated?
opts: One with triglycerides over 1000 mg/dL
Triglycerides above 1000 mg/dL are the primary indication for a fibrate, not a contraindication.
One with a low HDL cholesterol
Low HDL (high-density lipoprotein) is a primary fibrate indication, since fibrates raise HDL by 10 to 35%.
One with existing gallbladder disease
Correct. Fibrate contraindications are pregnancy, severe hepatic or renal dysfunction, and existing gallbladder disease; cholelithiasis is also an adverse effect.
One with well-controlled diabetes
Diabetes is a relative contraindication to niacin, not to fibrates. Existing gallbladder disease contraindicates fibrates.

set1.q: A 61-year-old man with stable angina has a history of hives and wheezing after taking aspirin. Which drug should replace aspirin to prevent acute coronary syndrome?
opts: Enoxaparin
It is an injectable anticoagulant used in acute coronary syndrome, not a long-term oral replacement for aspirin.
Isosorbide mononitrate
A nitrate treats symptoms and does not prevent acute coronary syndrome, so it cannot stand in for an antiplatelet.
Clopidogrel
Correct. It is as effective as aspirin for secondary prevention and is recommended when a patient is allergic to aspirin.
Metoprolol
It lowers demand and helps after an infarction, but it is not an antiplatelet and does not replace aspirin.

set1.q: A 54-year-old man with an acute coronary syndrome still has chest pain after aspirin. Blood pressure is 130/82 mmHg and he takes no phosphodiesterase-5 inhibitor. Which drug relieves his pain but does not improve survival?
opts: Aspirin
It reduces mortality, reinfarction and stroke, so it is a survival therapy and not just an analgesic.
Metoprolol
It lowers heart rate and oxygen demand and is given for outcome benefit, not as a drug whose only job is pain relief.
Clopidogrel
An antiplatelet that reduces clotting events. It does not relieve pain.
Nitroglycerin
Correct. Nitrates give chest pain relief with no mortality benefit, starting sublingually and moving to an intravenous infusion in hospital.

set1.q: A 57-year-old man with ST-elevation myocardial infarction still rates his pain 9 out of 10 after repeated sublingual nitroglycerin. Blood pressure is 124/76 mmHg. Which drug is used for chest pain unresponsive to nitrates?
opts: Metoprolol
It lowers heart rate and oxygen demand and is given for outcome benefit; it is not the analgesic for pain that persists despite nitrates.
Clopidogrel
An antiplatelet, it reduces clotting events and does not treat pain.
Enoxaparin
An anticoagulant that limits clot propagation, it has no analgesic effect.
Morphine
Correct. It is the opioid analgesic used for pain unresponsive to nitrates in ST-elevation infarction, though its use is controversial.

set1.q: A 65-year-old man with stable angina has type 2 diabetes mellitus and a reduced ejection fraction of 35 percent. He takes aspirin and metoprolol. Which added drug may slow progression of his coronary disease?
opts: An angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitor
Correct. It is used in coronary disease with diabetes or left ventricular systolic dysfunction and may prevent disease progression, though it does not relieve angina.
A long-acting nitrate
It relieves angina but does not slow progression of coronary disease, and it is an adjunct rather than a vasculoprotective drug.
A dihydropyridine calcium channel blocker
It treats symptoms and does not alter disease progression. With reduced ejection fraction, amlodipine is the calcium channel blocker that is accepted.
A non-dihydropyridine calcium channel blocker
With a reduced ejection fraction it is contraindicated, because it depresses contractility and can worsen heart failure.

set1.q: A 63-year-old man has three hours of chest pressure. The electrocardiogram shows ST-segment depression, and the cardiac biomarker is elevated. He has no bleeding history. Which therapy is not recommended for him?
opts: Aspirin
It is used in both ST-elevation and non-ST-elevation syndromes and reduces mortality and reinfarction.
Metoprolol
Beta blockers are common therapy for both syndromes when no contraindication exists.
Reteplase
Correct. Fibrinolytics are not recommended in non-ST-elevation acute coronary syndrome, because the bleeding risk outweighs the benefit.
Enoxaparin
It is a recommended anticoagulant in non-ST-elevation acute coronary syndrome, so it is not the therapy to withhold.

set1.q: A 57-year-old man with hypertension and stable angina has a blood pressure of 154/94 mmHg and a heart rate of 82 beats per minute. His clinician plans a calcium channel blocker. Which calcium channel blocker should be avoided?
opts: Long-acting nifedipine
The extended-release form gives a smooth, sustained effect without the abrupt drop in pressure, so it is acceptable when combined with a beta blocker.
Short-acting nifedipine
Correct. Its abrupt vasodilation causes hypotension and reflex tachycardia, which can worsen ischemia, so short-acting agents are avoided in angina.
Amlodipine
A long-acting dihydropyridine with a steady effect and little change in heart rate, so it is an appropriate choice rather than one to avoid.
Felodipine
A long-acting dihydropyridine, acceptable for angina. It is the short-acting nifedipine preparation, not this class, that is the concern.

set1.q: A 70-year-old man with stable angina opened his bottle of sublingual nitroglycerin tablets eight months ago. He keeps it in the original container in a bedroom drawer and has used it twice. In the traditional counseling, what should he be told about the tablets?
opts: Keep using them until the bottle is empty
Nitroglycerin is unstable, and waiting for the bottle to empty risks a degraded tablet in an emergency; the traditional advice is to replace opened tablets every 3 to 6 months.
Move them to a weekly pill organizer
The tablets belong in the original packaging in a cool, dry place, because light and moisture degrade them; a pill organizer is the wrong storage.
Refrigerate them to extend their life
Refrigeration is not the instruction; the tablets are kept cool and dry in the original packaging and replaced about every 3 to 6 months.
Replace them with a fresh supply

Correct. The traditional counseling is to replace opened tablets about every 3 to 6 months so that a potent tablet is ready in an emergency. Current labeling ties expiry to the printed date when the tablets stay in the tightly closed original glass bottle.

set1.q: A 64-year-old man with known angina develops chest pressure at rest. He sits down and places one nitroglycerin tablet under his tongue. Five minutes later the pain is unchanged. What should he do next?
opts: Call emergency services
Correct. Chest pain unrelieved five minutes after the first nitroglycerin dose is treated as a possible acute coronary syndrome, so emergency help is called.
Wait an hour to see if rest helps
Waiting delays care for what may be an infarction. The instruction is to call emergency services when the first dose has not relieved the pain.
Swallow a long-acting nitrate tablet
Long-acting nitrates are prophylactic adjuncts with a slow onset and are not rescue therapy for an attack that has not responded.
Take his beta blocker early
A beta blocker lowers demand over time and does not rescue an unrelieved attack. Emergency services are needed first.

set1.q: When left ventricular function is decreased and a beta blocker cannot be used, which calcium channel blocker is the alternative?
opts: Verapamil
Non-dihydropyridines such as verapamil are avoided when left ventricular function is decreased, since they depress contractility.
Amlodipine
Correct. Beta blockers are first line with decreased left ventricular function; amlodipine is the calcium channel blocker alternative.
Diltiazem
Diltiazem lowers contractility and heart rate, so it is avoided with decreased left ventricular function; amlodipine is the alternative.
Nifedipine
Calcium channel blockers other than amlodipine are avoided with decreased left ventricular function, and nifedipine's short-acting form is avoided in angina anyway.
